questions.q: In the example workflow, why does it trigger on both `push` to main and `pull_request` targeting main?
options: It's a mistake — only one trigger should ever be used
Because GitHub requires at least two triggers per workflow
So tests run once while the PR is open, letting reviewers see pass/fail, and again after the change actually merges
To make the workflow run twice as slowly on purpose
questions.explain: Triggering on both events means reviewers see test results before approving, and the merged code on main is verified again after merge.

questions.q: What does a red X status icon on a specific commit mean?
options: The commit was deleted
That specific commit's automated checks (such as tests) failed
The commit was never pushed
The repository itself has been disabled
questions.explain: A status icon is tied to a specific commit's workflow run results, not a vague general warning about the repository.

questions.q: What does a pull request's Checks tab show?
options: The PR author's commit history on unrelated repositories
Only the PR's title and description
A list of every other open PR in the repository
A rolled-up view of every workflow run triggered by that PR's commits, in one place
questions.explain: The Checks tab aggregates every check that ran against a PR's commits, letting you inspect any individual commit's results.

questions.q: By default, what happens when a status check fails on a pull request?
options: GitHub automatically closes the pull request
The failing commit is automatically deleted
It's only a visual indicator (a red X) — nothing stops the PR from being merged anyway unless branch protection requires that check
The repository's main branch is automatically locked forever
questions.explain: Without a required status check configured via branch protection, a failing check is purely informational and doesn't block merging.

questions.q: What turns a status check from a visual indicator into something that actually blocks a merge?
options: Deleting the failing commit manually
Simply having any workflow file in the repository
Nothing can ever block a merge on GitHub
A branch protection rule marking that specific check as required
questions.explain: A required status check, configured through branch protection rules, is what actually disables the merge button until the check passes.
